name: Vorozole

lead: Vorozole is an oral aromatase inhibitor developed for cancer. It occasionally comes up in physique forums as an estrogen blocker, with the aim of less water retention and a leaner look.

It competitively blocks the aromatase enzyme, reducing estrogen synthesis. Development stopped after a trial showed no survival difference from megestrol acetate, and it was never marketed. Today it is best known as a carbon-11 PET tracer for mapping aromatase in the human brain. No trial has tested it for appearance.

paras: It is not a marketed product. Its present use is as a research radiotracer in brain imaging.
Sources do not describe its adverse effects. It is an investigational compound without marketing approval.

angle.text: Vorozole is an aromatase inhibitor that occasionally comes up as an estrogen blocker: less estrogen synthesis means less water retention and a leaner look. It was studied for cancer and is now a brain-imaging tracer, and nothing has been tested for looks.

lead: Vorozole (developmental code R-76713, tentative brand name Rizivor, also spelled Rivizor) is a triazole-based, third-generation nonsteroidal aromatase inhibitor that was developed as a breast cancer drug. Aromatase is the enzyme that converts androgens to estrogens, so inhibiting it lowers estradiol. In physique and anabolic-steroid communities, aromatase inhibitors as a class are discussed as a way to limit estrogen-related effects such as water retention and gynecomastia, which affect how lean and defined a physique looks.[1][2]

Clinical development stopped after trials comparing it with other breast cancer therapies; Wikipedia reports that a comparison with megestrol acetate found no difference in median survival, and anastrozole, letrozole and exemestane became the standard agents.[1] A 1997 review of phase II and phase III studies described objective responses in up to 35 percent of patients and favourable efficacy compared with aminoglutethimide and megestrol at 2.5 mg per day.[3]

It is now best known in research as a radiotracer: carbon-11 labelled vorozole has been used with PET to map aromatase in the human brain.[4] Vorozole was never marketed, and no published trial has tested it for appearance, muscle or body-composition outcomes.

paras: Vorozole's investigated medical use was advanced breast cancer in postmenopausal women, where lowering estradiol slows estrogen-dependent tumours.[1][3][5] Its practical use today is as the carbon-11 labelled PET tracer for aromatase in brain imaging research.[4]

For appearance, the relevant context is the aromatase inhibitor class. T Nation discussions of estradiol cover why people monitor it and how aromatase inhibitors fit in with androgen use, and one thread's excerpt lists vorozole among type II aromatase inhibitors that bind the enzyme reversibly.[6][7]

The appearance angle is therefore indirect and class-based: aromatase inhibitors lower estradiol, and bodybuilding forums discuss that effect in connection with water retention and breast tissue growth, both of which change how defined a physique looks. Vorozole itself was not marketed, and the forum material that mentions it does so as one example within the inhibitor family.[6][7]

Vorozole binds the cytochrome P450 moiety of aromatase and causes reversible inhibition of the enzyme.[3][8] A review of its preclinical pharmacology reported that most activity comes from the dextro-isomer, with in vitro IC50 values of 1.38 nM against human placental aromatase and 0.44 nM in rat ovarian granulosa cells, selectivity for aromatase over other cytochrome P450 reactions, and no agonist or antagonist effects at estrogen, progestin, androgen or glucocorticoid receptors at up to 10 microM.[8] It is classified among type II aromatase inhibitors with anastrozole, letrozole, fadrozole and others.[7]
Wikipedia describes very high oral bioavailability, hepatic metabolism and a half-life of about 8 hours.[1]
It acts as a competitive inhibitor of aromatase and is metabolised in the liver; the molar mass is about 324.8 g/mol.[1]

In a phase II randomized, double-blind study of 24 postmenopausal women with advanced breast cancer who had relapsed on tamoxifen, doses of 1, 2.5 and 5 mg for a month each cut median serum estradiol by 91, 90 and 89 percent, and reduced estrone and estrone sulfate; the study found no significant effect on testosterone, androstenedione, aldosterone or thyroid-stimulating hormone.[9] In presurgical patients, vorozole reduced tissue estrone and estradiol by 64 and 80 percent respectively, and another trial compared its systemic and intratumoral effects with tamoxifen over 12 weeks.[8][10]

A 1993 randomized trial in healthy postmenopausal women examined inhibition of the conversion of androstenedione to estrone by vorozole.[11] These studies were all in women; no studies in men's physique outcomes were found.

A 1997 review reported that the most common adverse events with vorozole were hot flushes and nausea, generally mild, and that it was at least as well tolerated as megestrol, which caused more inappropriate weight gain, and better tolerated than aminoglutethimide.[3] Sources give little else on safety, as the drug never reached the market.

Vorozole was developed as a third-generation aromatase inhibitor in the early 1990s, with pharmacology and phase II studies published between 1993 and 1998.[8][9][11][12] Trials compared it with aminoglutethimide, megestrol and tamoxifen. Reviews in 2001 and 2020 place it among the third-generation inhibitors that preceded or were overtaken by anastrozole, letrozole and exemestane.[2][13][14]

Wikipedia records that clinical testing of vorozole as an antineoplastic agent was halted after trials showed no difference in median survival compared with the progestational agent megestrol acetate, and that research attention moved to the other third-generation aromatase inhibitors, anastrozole, letrozole and exemestane.[1] The page cites a 1998 review by Goss in Breast Cancer Research and Treatment for this account and notes the tentative brand name Rizivor was never used commercially.[1]

PET studies with [11C]vorozole reported a distinctive distribution of aromatase in the human brain.[4] Animal studies used vorozole to examine aromatase effects on male reproductive behaviour in Japanese quail.[15] A 1996 review lists aromatase inhibitors among agents explored for cancer chemoprevention.[16]

Phase II and phase III trials in postmenopausal advanced breast cancer examined vorozole at doses around 2.5 mg per day, reporting objective response rates of roughly 18 to 35 percent in phase II studies and comparisons with aminoglutethimide and megestrol in phase III.[3][8] An EORTC study examined the relationship between serum vorozole levels and clinical results.[17] A randomized presurgical trial compared vorozole with tamoxifen.[10] Imaging studies in humans used it as a tracer rather than a treatment.[4] No studies were found testing vorozole for appearance, muscle or body composition.

lore.intro: Vorozole itself is rarely discussed in physique communities; threads about estradiol and aromatase inhibitors occasionally mention it as one of the class.[6][7]
